FINE PARALLEL PROCESSING USING A WORK QUEUE
================================================================================

In this example, you will run a Kubernetes Job that runs multiple parallel
tasks as worker processes, each running as a separate Pod.

In this example, as each pod is created, it picks up one unit of work
from a task queue, processes it, and repeats until the end of the queue is reached.

OVERVIEW OF STEPS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Start a storage service to hold the work queue. (We will use Redis).
2. Create a queue, and fill it with messages.
3. Start a Job that works on tasks from the queue.

BEFORE YOU BEGIN
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
You need to have a Kubernetes cluster, and the kubectl command-line tool must
be configured.

You will need a container image registry (like Docker Hub) where you can upload 
images to run in your cluster.

Documentation Link: https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/job/fine-parallel-processing-work-queue/

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 1: STARTING REDIS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
For this example, you will start a single instance of Redis.

Run the following commands:

kubectl apply -f https://k8s.io/examples/application/job/redis/redis-pod.yaml
    kubectl apply -f https://k8s.io/examples/application/job/redis/redis-service.yaml

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 2: FILLING THE QUEUE WITH TASKS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Start a temporary interactive pod for running the Redis CLI:

kubectl run -i --tty temp --image redis --command "/bin/sh"

Once the prompt appears, connect to Redis and fill the queue (named "job2"):

redis-cli -h redis

# Inside the redis prompt:
    rpush job2 "apple"
    rpush job2 "banana"
    rpush job2 "cherry"
    rpush job2 "date"
    rpush job2 "fig"
    rpush job2 "grape"
    rpush job2 "lemon"
    rpush job2 "melon"
    rpush job2 "orange"

# Check the list:
    lrange job2 0 -1

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 3: CREATE A CONTAINER IMAGE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
You need a Python worker program to read from the queue.

Here is the worker script (worker.py):

#!/usr/bin/env python
    import time
    import rediswq

host="redis"
    # Uncomment next two lines if you do not have Kube-DNS working.
    # import os
    # host = os.getenv("REDIS_SERVICE_HOST")

q = rediswq.RedisWQ(name="job2", host=host)
    print("Worker with sessionID: " +  q.sessionID())
    print("Initial queue state: empty=" + str(q.empty()))
    while not q.empty():
      item = q.lease(lease_secs=10, block=True, timeout=2) 
      if item is not None:
        itemstr = item.decode("utf-8")
        print("Working on " + itemstr)
        time.sleep(10) # Put your actual work here instead of sleep.
        q.complete(item)
      else:
        print("Waiting for work")
    print("Queue empty, exiting")

Build the image (requires Docker):

docker build -t job-wq-2 .

Push the image to your registry (replace <username> with your Hub username):

docker tag job-wq-2 <username>/job-wq-2
    docker push <username>/job-wq-2

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 4: DEFINING A JOB
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Here is the manifest for the Job (job.yaml). 
Note: Replace "gcr.io/myproject" with your image registry path.

apiVersion: batch/v1
    kind: Job
    metadata:
      name: job-wq-2
    spec:
      parallelism: 2
      template:
        metadata:
          name: job-wq-2
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: c
            image: gcr.io/myproject/job-wq-2
          restartPolicy: OnFailure

Note on Parallelism:
In this example, each pod works on several items from the queue and then exits. 
Workers signal the queue is empty by exiting with success.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 5: RUNNING THE JOB
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Run the Job:

kubectl apply -f ./job.yaml

Check on the Job:

kubectl describe jobs/job-wq-2

Wait for the Job to succeed:

kubectl wait --for=condition=complete --timeout=300s job/job-wq-2

Check logs to see the work being done:

kubectl logs pods/job-wq-2-xxxxx

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ALTERNATIVES
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
If you have a continuous stream of background processing work to run, consider 
running your background workers with a ReplicaSet instead.

Consider using a background processing library such as Resque:
https://github.com/resque/resque

Automate job creation and management

This article shows you how to get started with developer tools to automate the creation and management of jobs. It introduces you to the Databricks CLI, the Databricks SDKs, and the REST API.

Compare tools

The following table compares the Databricks CLI, the Databricks SDKs, and the REST API for programmatically creating and managing jobs. To learn about all available developer tools, see Local development tools .

Tool

Description

Databricks CLI

Access Databricks functionality using the Databricks command-line interface (CLI), which wraps the REST API. Use the CLI for one-off tasks such as experimentation, shell scripting, and invoking the REST API directly.

Databricks SDKs

Develop applications and create custom Databricks workflows using a Databricks SDK, available for Python, Java, Go, or R. Instead of sending REST API calls directly using curl or Postman, you can use an SDK to interact with Databricks.

Databricks REST API

If none of the above options work for your specific use case, you can use the Databricks REST API directly. Use the REST API directly for use cases such as automating processes where an SDK in your preferred programming language is not currently available.

Get started with the Databricks CLI

To install and configure authentication for the Databricks CLI, see Install or update the Databricks CLI and Authentication for the Databricks CLI .

The Databricks CLI has command groups for Databricks features, including one for jobs, that contain a set of related commands. The jobs command group enables you to manage your jobs and job runs with actions such as create , delete , and get . Because the CLI wraps the Databricks REST API, most CLI commands map to a REST API request. For example, databricks jobs get maps to GET/api/2.2/jobs/get .

To output more detailed usage and syntax information for the jobs command group, use the -h flag:

databricks jobs -h

databricks jobs <command-name> -h

databricks jobs <command-name> <subcommand-name> -h

Run a job using the CLI

There are three ways to run your job when using the command line.

Scheduled . If the job definition (in JSON) includes a schedule, then the job will automatically run on the schedule.

Trigger with run-now . The databricks jobs run-now CLI command triggers a run for a job that you have already created.

Trigger with submit . The databricks jobs submit CLI command takes a job definition and triggers a run for the job. With submit , the job is not saved, and isn't visible in the UI. It runs once, and when it is done, it no longer exists as a job.

Get started with the Databricks SDK

Databricks provides SDKs that allow you to automate operations using popular programming languages such as Python, Java, and Go. This section shows you how to get started using the Python SDK to create and manage jobs on Databricks.

You can use the Databricks SDK from your Databricks notebook or from your local development machine. If you are using your local development machine, ensure you first complete Get started with the Databricks SDK for Python .

Run a job using the Python SDK

There are three ways to run a job when using the API.

Scheduled . If the job definition (in JSON) includes a schedule, then the job will automatically run on the schedule.

Trigger with run-now . The jobs.run_now API triggers a run for a job that you have already created.

Trigger with submit . The jobs.runs.submit API takes a job definition and triggers a run for the job.

Get started with the Databricks REST API

The following example makes a request to the Databricks REST API to retrieve details for a single job. It assumes the DATABRICKS_HOST and DATABRICKS_TOKEN environment variables have been set as described in Perform personal access token authentication .

For information on using the Databricks REST API see the Databricks REST API reference documentation .

View jobs as code

From the Databricks workspace you can view the JSON, YAML, or Python representation of a job.

In your Databricks workspace's sidebar, click Jobs & Pipelines and select a job.

Click the kebab to the left of the Run now button, then click View as code :

Click YAML , Python , or JSON to view the job as code in that language. For YAML, click Copy , then paste the code directly into Databricks Asset Bundles configuration *.yaml files to include the existing job in a bundle. For Python, choose Databricks SDK or Databricks Asset Bundles , then click Copy . The Python code for the SDK can be used to create the job in notebooks or locally when using the Databricks Python SDK . The Python code for bundles can be used to include the job in a bundle using Python. See Bundle configuration in Python . For JSON, click Copy and use the code to create, update, or get the job using the Databricks CLI , the Databricks SDKs , or the Databricks REST API .

Clean up

To delete any jobs you just created, run databricks jobs delete <job-id> from the Databricks CLI or delete the job directly from the Databricks workspace UI.

Mastering Kubernetes Jobs and CronJobs: A Platform Engineer’s Complete Guide

Introduction

As a platform engineer, you’ve likely encountered scenarios where you need to run one-time tasks, batch jobs, or scheduled operations in your Kubernetes clusters. Unlike long-running services managed by Deployments or StatefulSets, these finite workloads require a different approach. Enter Kubernetes Jobs and CronJobs — powerful resources designed specifically for task-oriented workloads that run to completion.

In this comprehensive guide, we’ll explore everything you need to know about Jobs and CronJobs, from basic concepts to advanced patterns, real-world use cases, troubleshooting strategies, and security considerations.

Kubernetes Job Hierarchy

Understanding Kubernetes Jobs

What Are Jobs?

A Kubernetes Job is a resource designed to run finite workloads that execute a task to completion. Unlike Pods created via Deployments, which run indefinitely, a Job ensures that its associated Pods complete their task and then exit successfully.

Key Characteristics

1. Restart Policy Requirements

Jobs have strict requirements for Pod restart policies:

OnFailure: Kubelet restarts the container within the same Pod if it crashes.

Never: Entire Pod is marked as failed, Job controller creates a new Pod.

Always: Not allowed (would prevent Pod from ever completing).

2. API Group and Immutability

Belongs to the batch/v1 API group (stable).

Pod template cannot be modified after Job creation.

Immutable by design for consistency.

Job Lifecycle States

Creating Your First Job

Here’s a basic Job manifest example:

apiVersion: batch/v1

kind: Job

metadata:

name: data-processor

namespace: batch-jobs

spec:

template:

spec:

containers:

- name: processor

image: mcr.microsoft.com/powershell:7.2-alpine-3.13

command:

- pwsh

- -Command

- |

Write-Host "Starting data processing at $(Get-Date)"

Start-Sleep -Seconds 30

Write-Host "Processing completed at $(Get-Date)"

resources:

requests:

cpu: 500m

memory: 200Mi

limits:

cpu: 600m

memory: 300Mi

restartPolicy: Never

backoffLimit: 3

Job Manifest Breakdown

Advanced Job Patterns

Completions and Parallelism

Two critical fields control how Jobs execute:

Completions

Specifies the number of Pods that must successfully complete:

spec:

completions: 5  # Job completes after 5 successful Pod completions

Parallelism

Controls maximum concurrent Pods:

spec:

parallelism: 3  # Max 3 Pods running simultaneously

Parallel Job Execution Timeline

Job Completion Modes

NonIndexed (Default)

All Pods are identical:

spec:

completionMode: NonIndexed

completions: 3

parallelism: 2

Indexed Mode

Each Pod gets a unique completion index:

spec:

completionMode: Indexed

completions: 3

parallelism: 2

template:

spec:

containers:

- name: worker

image: alpine:latest

command:

- sh

- -c

- |

echo "Processing index: $JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX"

# Process specific data slice based on index

NonIndexed vs Indexed Comparison

Understanding CronJobs

What Are CronJobs?

A CronJob is a thin wrapper around Jobs that enables scheduling. It creates Job objects automatically based on a defined schedule using the familiar cron format.

CronJob Architecture Flow

Schedule Configuration

The schedule field uses the standard cron format:

# ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59)

# │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23)

# │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31)

# │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12)

# │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6) (Sunday to Saturday)

# │ │ │ │ │

# * * * * *

Common Schedule Examples:

# Every minute

schedule: "* * * * *"

# Every hour at minute 0

schedule: "0 * * * *"

# Daily at 2:30 AM

schedule: "30 2 * * *"

# Every Monday at 9:00 AM

schedule: "0 9 * * 1"

# Every 15 minutes

schedule: "*/15 * * * *"

# Shorthand expressions

schedule: "@hourly"    # Every hour

schedule: "@daily"     # Every day at midnight

schedule: "@weekly"    # Every Sunday at midnight

schedule: "@monthly"   # First day of each month at midnight

schedule: "@yearly"    # January 1st at midnight

Cron Expression Guide

Complete CronJob Example:

apiVersion: batch/v1

kind: CronJob

metadata:

name: database-backup

namespace: production

spec:

schedule: "0 2 * * *"  # Daily at 2 AM

timeZone: "America/New_York"

jobTemplate:

metadata:

labels:

app: db-backup

type: maintenance

spec:

template:

metadata:

labels:

app: db-backup

type: maintenance

spec:

containers:

- name: backup-tool

image: postgres:13-alpine

command:

- sh

- -c

- |

pg_dump -h $DB_HOST -U $DB_USER -d $DB_NAME > /backup/backup-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).sql

echo "Backup completed successfully"

env:

- name: DB_HOST

value: "postgres.database.svc.cluster.local"

- name: DB_USER

valueFrom:

secretKeyRef:

name: db-credentials

key: username

- name: DB_NAME

value: "production_db"

volumeMounts:

- name: backup-storage

mountPath: /backup

resources:

requests:

cpu: 200m

memory: 256Mi

limits:

cpu: 500m

memory: 512Mi

securityContext:

runAsNonRoot: true

runAsUser: 999

readOnlyRootFilesystem: true

volumes:

- name: backup-storage

persistentVolumeClaim:

claimName: backup-pvc

restartPolicy: OnFailure

backoffLimit: 3

activeDeadlineSeconds: 3600  # 1 hour timeout

successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3

failedJobsHistoryLimit: 5

concurrencyPolicy: Forbid

startingDeadlineSeconds: 300

Real-World Use Cases and Patterns

1. Data Processing Pipeline

Scenario: Daily ETL job processing customer data

kind: CronJob

metadata:

name: etl-customer-data

spec:

schedule: "0 1 * * *"  # Daily at 1 AM

spec:

value: "$(date -d 'yesterday' +%Y-%m-%d)"

- name: BATCH_SIZE

value: "1000"

requests:

cpu: 1000m

memory: 2Gi

limits:

cpu: 2000m

memory: 4Gi

restartPolicy: OnFailure

backoffLimit: 2

failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3

2. Database Maintenance

Scenario: Weekly database cleanup and optimization

apiVersion: batch/v1

kind: CronJob

metadata:

name: db-maintenance

spec:

schedule: "0 3 * * 0"  # Sundays at 3 AM

jobTemplate:

spec:

template:

spec:

containers:

- name: db-maintenance

image: postgres:13-alpine

command:

- sh

- -c

- |

# Cleanup old logs

psql -c "DELETE FROM application_logs WHERE created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days';"

# Rebuild indexes

psql -c "REINDEX DATABASE $DB_NAME;"

# Update statistics

psql -c "ANALYZE;"

echo "Maintenance completed"

envFrom:

- secretRef:

name: db-connection-secret

restartPolicy: OnFailure

activeDeadlineSeconds: 7200  # 2 hours max

command: ["python", "train_model.py"]

mountPath: /data

mountPath: /models

Monitoring and Observability

Monitoring Job Health

Kubernetes Job Metrics Dashboard

Key Metrics to Track

1. Job Success Rate

# Prometheus query

rate(kube_job_status_succeeded[5m]) / rate(kube_job_status_completed[5m])

2. Job Duration

# Average job duration

avg(kube_job_status_completion_time - kube_job_status_start_time)

3. Failed Jobs

# Count of failed jobs

increase(kube_job_status_failed[1h])

Logging Best Practices

Implement structured logging in your job containers:

import logging

import json

from datetime import datetime

class StructuredLogger:

def __init__(self, job_name):

self.job_name = job_name

self.logger = logging.getLogger(job_name)

def log(self, level, message, **kwargs):

log_data = {

"timestamp": datetime.utcnow().isoformat(),

"job_name": self.job_name,

"level": level,

"message": message,

**kwargs

}

self.logger.info(json.dumps(log_data))

# Usage in job container

logger = StructuredLogger("data-processor")

logger.log("INFO", "Processing started", batch_size=1000)

logger.log("ERROR", "Processing failed", error_code="DB_CONNECTION_ERROR")

Alerting Strategy

Create alerts for critical job failures:

groups:

name: kubernetes-jobs

rules:

- alert: JobFailed

expr: kube_job_status_failed > 0

for: 0m

labels:

severity: warning

annotations:

summary: "Job {{ $labels.job_name }} failed"

description: "Job {{ $labels.job_name }} in namespace {{ $labels.namespace }} has failed"

- alert: CronJobMissing

expr: |

(time() - kube_cronjob_status_last_schedule_time) > 3600

and kube_cronjob_spec_suspend == 0

for: 5m

labels:

severity: critical

annotations:

summary: "CronJob {{ $labels.cronjob }} hasn't run in over an hour"

Troubleshooting Common Issues

1. Job Stuck in Pending State

Symptoms: Job created but no Pods are running

Common Causes:

Insufficient cluster resources

Node selector constraints

Pod security policies blocking creation

Diagnostic Commands:

# Check job status

kubectl describe job <job-name>

# Check events

kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp

# Check resource availability

kubectl top nodes

kubectl describe nodes

Solution Example:

# Add resource requests to help scheduler

spec:

template:

spec:

containers:

- name: job-container

resources:

requests:

cpu: 100m

memory: 128Mi

limits:

cpu: 500m

memory: 512Mi

2. CronJob Not Creating Jobs

Symptoms: CronJob exists but no Jobs are created

CronJob Troubleshooting Flowchart

Diagnostic Steps:

# Check CronJob status

kubectl describe cronjob <cronjob-name>

# Verify schedule syntax

# Use online cron expression testers

# Check controller manager logs

kubectl logs -n kube-system deployment/kube-controller-manager

Common Issues:

# Issue: Invalid cron expression

schedule: "60 * * * *"  # Invalid - minute must be 0-59

# Fix: Correct expression

schedule: "0 * * * *"   # Every hour at minute 0

# Issue: Timezone problems

schedule: "0 9 * * *"   # Runs at 9 AM in cluster timezone

# Fix: Specify timezone

spec:

timeZone: "America/New_York"

schedule: "0 9 * * *"  # Runs at 9 AM Eastern Time

3. Jobs Failing Due to Resource Limits

Symptoms: Pods getting OOMKilled or CPU throttled

Diagnostic Commands:

# Check pod resource usage

kubectl top pod <pod-name>

# Check pod events for OOMKilled

kubectl describe pod <pod-name>

# Check resource quotas

kubectl describe quota -n <namespace>

Solutions:

# Increase resource limits

spec:

template:

spec:

containers:

- name: resource-hungry-job

resources:

requests:

cpu: 1000m

memory: 2Gi

limits:

cpu: 2000m

memory: 4Gi

# Or use vertical pod autoscaling for right-sizing

apiVersion: autoscaling.k8s.io/v1

kind: VerticalPodAutoscaler

metadata:

name: job-vpa

spec:

targetRef:

apiVersion: batch/v1

kind: Job

name: my-job

updatePolicy:

updateMode: "Initial"  # Only set resources for new pods

4. Jobs Taking Too Long

Symptoms: Jobs running longer than expected

Solutions:

# Set active deadline

spec:

activeDeadlineSeconds: 3600  # Kill job after 1 hour

# Increase parallelism for parallelizable workloads

spec:

parallelism: 5

completions: 10

# Use faster nodes with node affinity

spec:

template:

spec:

affinity:

nodeAffinity:

requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:

nodeSelectorTerms:

- matchExpressions:

- key: node-type

operator: In

values: ["high-performance"]

Performance Optimization

1. Resource Right-Sizing

Performance Optimization Charts

Use Vertical Pod Autoscaler recommendations:

# Install VPA if not present

kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes/autoscaler/releases/download/vpa-0.13.0/vpa-release-0.13.0.yaml

# Create VPA for job analysis

kubectl apply -f - <<EOF

kind: VerticalPodAutoscaler

metadata:

name: job-sizing-analysis

spec:

targetRef:

kind: Job

name: my-analysis-job

updatePolicy:

updateMode: "Off"  # Just provide recommendations

EOF

# Check recommendations

kubectl describe vpa job-sizing-analysis

2. Efficient Container Images

# Multi-stage build for smaller images

FROM golang:1.19-alpine AS builder

WORKDIR /app

COPY go.mod go.sum ./

RUN go mod download

COPY . .

RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux go build -o job-runner

FROM alpine:3.16

RUN apk --no-cache add ca-certificates

WORKDIR /root/

COPY --from=builder /app/job-runner .

USER 1000:1000

CMD ["./job-runner"]

3. Parallel Processing Patterns

# Pattern 1: Fixed work distribution

apiVersion: batch/v1

kind: Job

metadata:

name: parallel-processing

spec:

completions: 10

parallelism: 3

completionMode: Indexed

template:

spec:

containers:

- name: worker

image: my-app:latest

command:

- sh

- -c

- |

START_INDEX=$((JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX * 1000))

END_INDEX=$(((JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX + 1) * 1000 - 1))

./process-data --start=$START_INDEX --end=$END_INDEX

4. Storage Optimization

# Use appropriate storage classes

apiVersion: v1

kind: PersistentVolumeClaim

metadata:

name: job-fast-storage

spec:

import os

import hashlib

def process_data_idempotently(data_path, output_path):

# Create checksum of input data

input_hash = hashlib.md5(open(data_path, 'rb').read()).hexdigest()

# Check if output already exists with same input hash

metadata_file = f"{output_path}.metadata"

if os.path.exists(output_path) and os.path.exists(metadata_file):

with open(metadata_file, 'r') as f:

existing_hash = f.read().strip()

if existing_hash == input_hash:

print("Output already exists for this input, skipping...")

return

# Process data

result = expensive_processing(data_path)

# Save result and metadata atomically

temp_output = f"{output_path}.tmp"

with open(temp_output, 'w') as f:

f.write(result)

os.rename(temp_output, output_path)

with open(metadata_file, 'w') as f:

f.write(input_hash)

3. Graceful Shutdown Handling

import signal

import sys

import time

class GracefulJobRunner:

def __init__(self):

self.shutdown_requested = False

signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, self.signal_handler)

signal.signal(signal.SIGINT, self.signal_handler)

def signal_handler(self, signum, frame):

print(f"Received signal {signum}, initiating graceful shutdown...")

self.shutdown_requested = True

def run(self):

items_to_process = self.get_work_items()

for item in items_to_process:

if self.shutdown_requested:

print("Shutdown requested, stopping gracefully...")

self.save_progress(item)

sys.exit(0)

self.process_item(item)

self.mark_completed(item)

print("All items processed successfully")

if __name__ == "__main__":

runner = GracefulJobRunner()

runner.run()

import unittest

import yaml

class JobTestCase(unittest.TestCase):

def setUp(self):

self.namespace = "test-jobs"

subprocess.run(f"kubectl create namespace {self.namespace}", shell=True)

def tearDown(self):

subprocess.run(f"kubectl delete namespace {self.namespace}", shell=True)

def test_job_completion(self):

# Apply job manifest

with open('test-job.yaml', 'r') as f:

job_manifest = yaml.safe_load(f)

job_manifest['metadata']['namespace'] = self.namespace

with open('temp-job.yaml', 'w') as f:

yaml.dump(job_manifest, f)

# Apply the job

result = subprocess.run("kubectl apply -f temp-job.yaml", shell=True, capture_output=True)

self.assertEqual(result.returncode, 0)

# Wait for completion

job_name = job_manifest['metadata']['name']

wait_cmd = f"kubectl wait --for=condition=complete job/{job_name} -n {self.namespace} --timeout=300s"

result = subprocess.run(wait_cmd, shell=True)

self.assertEqual(result.returncode, 0)

# Verify job succeeded

status_cmd = f"kubectl get job/{job_name} -n {self.namespace} -o jsonpath='{{.status.succeeded}}'"

result = subprocess.run(status_cmd, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True)

self.assertEqual(result.stdout.strip(), "1")

3. Data Recovery Procedures

#!/usr/bin/env python3

"""

Job Data Recovery Script

Recovers data from failed or incomplete jobs

"""

import subprocess

import json

import sys

from datetime import datetime, timedelta

class JobRecoveryManager:

def __init__(self, namespace="default"):

self.namespace = namespace

def find_failed_jobs(self, hours=24):

"""Find jobs that failed in the last N hours"""

since_time = datetime.now() - timedelta(hours=hours)

cmd = [

"kubectl", "get", "jobs",

f"--namespace={self.namespace}",

"--field-selector=status.failed>0",

"-o", "json"

]

result = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)

jobs = json.loads(result.stdout)

failed_jobs = []

for job in jobs['items']:

job_time = datetime.fromisoformat(

job['status']['startTime'].replace('Z', '+00:00')

)

if job_time >= since_time:

failed_jobs.append(job)

return failed_jobs

def recover_job_data(self, job_name):

"""Attempt to recover data from failed job"""

# Get job pods

cmd = [

"kubectl", "get", "pods",

f"--namespace={self.namespace}",

f"--selector=job-name={job_name}",

"-o", "json"

]

result = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)

pods = json.loads(result.stdout)

recovery_data = {}

for pod in pods['items']:

pod_name = pod['metadata']['name']

# Extract logs

log_cmd = ["kubectl", "logs", pod_name, f"--namespace={self.namespace}"]

log_result = subprocess.run(log_cmd, capture_output=True, text=True)

# Extract any output files

files_cmd = [

"kubectl", "exec", pod_name,

f"--namespace={self.namespace}",

"--", "find", "/output", "-type", "f"

]

files_result = subprocess.run(files_cmd, capture_output=True, text=True)

recovery_data[pod_name] = {

'logs': log_result.stdout,

'files': files_result.stdout.split('\n') if files_result.returncode == 0 else [],

'exit_code': pod.get('status', {}).get('containerStatuses', [{}])[0].get('state', {}).get('terminated', {}).get('exitCode')

}

return recovery_data

def create_recovery_job(self, original_job, recovery_point=None):

"""Create a new job to continue from recovery point"""

recovery_job = original_job.copy()

# Update metadata

recovery_job['metadata']['name'] = f"{original_job['metadata']['name']}-recovery-{int(datetime.now().timestamp())}"

recovery_job['metadata'].pop('uid', None)

recovery_job['metadata'].pop('resourceVersion', None)

# Add recovery environment variables

containers = recovery_job['spec']['template']['spec']['containers']

for container in containers:

env = container.get('env', [])

env.append({

'name': 'RECOVERY_MODE',

'value': 'true'

})

if recovery_point:

env.append({

'name': 'RECOVERY_POINT',

'value': str(recovery_point)

})

container['env'] = env

return recovery_job

if __name__ == "__main__":

manager = JobRecoveryManager()

failed_jobs = manager.find_failed_jobs()

for job in failed_jobs:

job_name = job['metadata']['name']

print(f"Recovering data from failed job: {job_name}")

recovery_data = manager.recover_job_data(job_name)

# Save recovery data

with open(f"{job_name}-recovery.json", 'w') as f:

json.dump(recovery_data, f, indent=2)
print(f"Recovery data saved to {job_name}-recovery.json")

HPA & VPA in Kubernetes by Anvesh Muppeda

In the world of container orchestration, Kubernetes has emerged as the de facto standard. One of its powerful features is autoscaling, which helps maintain application performance and optimize resource usage. In this post, we’ll dive into two main types of autoscaling in Kubernetes: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (HPA) and Vertical Pod Autoscaling (VPA) .

Introduction to Kubernetes Autoscaling

Autoscaling in Kubernetes ensures that your application can handle varying loads by automatically adjusting the number of running pods or the resources allocated to them. This dynamic adjustment is crucial for maintaining application performance, optimizing resource usage, and reducing operational costs.

HPA & VPA Animation

Metric Server Setup

Before testing Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) and Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) , it’s essential to have the Metrics Server installed in your Kubernetes cluster. The Metrics Server collects resource usage metrics from the cluster’s nodes and pods, which are necessary for autoscaling decisions.

You can install the Metrics Server using either a YAML manifest or the official Helm chart. To install the latest release of the Metrics Server from the YAML manifest, follow these steps:

Download the Components Manifest: Use kubectl apply to download and apply the Components manifest directly from the latest release of the Metrics Server:

This command fetches the YAML manifest for the latest release of the Metrics Server from its GitHub repository and applies it to your Kubernetes cluster.

2. Verify Installation: After applying the manifest, verify that the Metrics Server pods are running successfully. You can check the pods in the kube-system namespace:

Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (HPA)

What is HPA?

Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (HPA) automatically scales the number of pods in a replication controller, deployment, or replica set based on observed CPU utilization (or other select metrics). This allows your application to scale out (add more pods) or scale in (reduce the number of pods) in response to load changes.

How Does HPA Work?

HPA operates by:

Monitoring Metrics: HPA continuously monitors the specified metrics (e.g., CPU usage, memory usage, custom metrics).

Evaluating Thresholds: It compares the current metric values against predefined thresholds.

Scaling Pods: If the metric values exceed the thresholds, HPA increases the number of pods. Conversely, if the values drop below the thresholds, it decreases the number of pods.

Advantages of HPA

Elasticity : Automatically adjusts the number of pods to meet current demand.

Cost-Efficiency: Optimizes resource usage by adding or removing pods as needed.

Performance : Helps maintain application performance during high traffic periods.

Vertical Pod Autoscaling (VPA)

What is VPA?

Vertical Pod Autoscaling (VPA) adjusts the CPU and memory resource requests and limits for your pods. Instead of adding more pods, VPA modifies the resources allocated to existing pods.

How Does VPA Work?

VPA operates by:

Monitoring Resource Usage: VPA continuously monitors the CPU and memory usage of the pods.

Recommending Resources: Based on the usage patterns, VPA recommends resource adjustments.

Applying Changes: The VPA can automatically apply the recommended changes to the pod specifications, typically requiring a pod restart.

Advantages of VPA

Resource Optimization: Ensures pods have the right amount of resources, preventing over-provisioning or under-provisioning.

Simplified Resource Management: Reduces the need to manually adjust resource requests and limits.

Improved Performance: Helps maintain application performance by dynamically adjusting resources based on actual usage.

How VPA Adjusts Resources

Initial Adjustment: When the VPA first starts managing a pod, it ensures that the pod’s resource requests are within the specified minAllowed and maxAllowed ranges. In your case, the minAllowed CPU is set to 100m , so the VPA initially adjusts the pod's CPU request to at least 100m to ensure it has a minimum baseline of resources.

Ongoing Monitoring and Adjustment: After the initial adjustment, the VPA continues to monitor the CPU and memory usage of the pods. It collects data over time to understand the resource utilization patterns and make more informed recommendations.

Recommendation Based on Observed Usage: The VPA makes recommendations based on observed usage. It doesn’t immediately jump to the maximum allowed ( maxAllowed ) value unless the observed usage justifies it. Instead, it incrementally adjusts the resource requests to align closely with actual usage patterns.

HPA vs. VPA: Which One to Use?

Choosing between HPA and VPA depends on your application’s requirements:

HPA is ideal for stateless applications that can easily scale horizontally by adding more pods. It’s useful when you need to handle variable workloads and ensure high availability.

VPA is suitable for applications where scaling horizontally is not feasible or when you need to optimize resource usage for individual pods. It’s beneficial for stateful applications or those with varying resource needs.

Conclusion

Kubernetes autoscaling, through HPA and VPA, provides robust mechanisms to manage application scalability and resource optimization. By understanding and implementing these autoscaling strategies, you can ensure that your applications are resilient, performant, and cost-effective.
